definitions.definition: The absence of own-nature (svabhāva) in every dharma, which is the same as its dependent origination; it is a dependent designation and the middle way (MMK 24.18), is itself empty (13.7) and is not a view to be held (13.8).
The mere negation of own-nature, implying nothing positive in its place; taught as sixteen or twenty emptinesses (MA 6); realized also by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas (Candrakīrti).
The lack of own-nature of all things, established because nothing is truly one or truly many (MAL 1).

cross_language.note: in the Pali suttas chiefly emptiness of self; Madhyamaka extends it to all dharmas

definitions.definition: Empty of own-nature: said of every dharma because none is not dependently arisen (MMK 24.19); yet 'empty' itself is said only for the sake of designation and is not to be asserted as a thesis (22.11).
Emptiness is itself empty: if nothing were non-empty nothing could be empty (MMK 13.7); one of the sixteen emptinesses (MA 6), taught so that emptiness is not grasped as an entity.

cross_language.form: stong pa nyid stong pa nyid

definitions.definition: What a thing would have by itself: unfabricated (akṛtrima) and not dependent on anything else (MMK 15.1–2). Since whatever is produced by causes and conditions would be 'made', nothing has own-nature; the Ābhidharmikas' own-nature of dharmas is the chief target of the critique.
Nothing has own-nature even conventionally; conventional things are accepted only as the world accepts them, without analysis.

cross_language.note: in the Pali commentaries the 'own-characteristic' of a dhamma

definitions.definition: The absence of own-nature in all existents, synonymous with emptiness; existents without own-nature are dependently arisen (MMK 1.10; 17.21; 22.16).

cross_language.form: rang bzhin med pa / ngo bo nyid med pa

definitions.definition: The nature a thing would have in relation to another; since own-nature is not found, other-nature — which is only the own-nature of another — is not found either (MMK 1.3; 15.3).
One of the two defining marks of own-nature (with independence): what is not produced by causes and conditions (MMK 15.2).
A real existent or existence; with its opposite (abhāva) one of the two extremes: whoever sees existence and non-existence does not see the truth (MMK 15.6), and nirvāṇa is neither (25.4–10).
Non-existence is only the alteration of an existent; where no existent is established, non-existence is not established either (MMK 15.5); nirvāṇa is not a non-existence (25.7–8).

The arising of things in dependence on causes and conditions, which is their non-arising by own-nature: it is called emptiness, dependent designation and the middle way (MMK 24.18; PsP); taught in the dedication as free of the eight extremes and as the pacification of elaboration; conventionally the twelve links (MMK 26).

literal: designation in dependence (on parts or bases)

definitions.definition: Designation made in dependence on a basis, as a chariot is designated in dependence on its wheels and other parts; emptiness itself is such a designation (MMK 24.18; PsP on 24.18).

cross_language.note: Kumārajīva's rendering of prajñapti in MMK 24.18

definitions.definition: Conceptual and verbal designation; the self, the Tathāgata and even 'empty' exist only as designations made in dependence (MMK 9.3; 22.8; 22.11).
The path between the extremes of existence and non-existence, eternalism and annihilationism; identified with emptiness and dependent origination (MMK 24.18).

cross_language.note: in the first sermon the path between sensual indulgence and self-mortification

literal: the middle; (the doctrine of) the Middle

definitions.definition: The middle between all extremes; the name of Nāgārjuna's teaching and school, its followers being Mādhyamikas.

cross_language.form: 中觀 zhongguan / 中論 zhonglun

literal: one of the middle, follower of the Madhyamaka

definitions.definition: A follower of the Madhyamaka; 'for one who is a Mādhyamika it is not right to state an autonomous inference' (PsP 1).

literal: the doctrine of emptiness / of the void

definitions.definition: A name for the Madhyamaka used mostly by its opponents, who read it as the doctrine that nothing exists; the Mādhyamikas reject the nihilist reading (PsP 17.30; 18.7).
The conventional truth of the world and the truth of the ultimate, on which the Buddhas' teaching relies (MMK 24.8–10).
Every thing bears two natures, found by correct and by false seeing (MA 6.23); the intellect is conventional and reality is beyond its domain (BCA 9.2).
The truth of worldly convention (lokasaṃvṛti), relied on for teaching the ultimate (MMK 24.8–10).
Saṃvṛti is ignorance that totally covers reality, or mutual dependence, or worldly convention (PsP 24.8); what delusion fabricates and presents as true (MA 6.28).
Divided into the correct conventional, which functions as it appears, and the incorrect conventional, which does not (Jñānagarbha); the ladder to the ultimate (Bhāviveka).

cross_language.form: 世俗諦 shisudi / 俗諦 sudi

equivalents.note: Theravāda sammuti-sacca also denotes conventional designations, but it contrasts with ultimately real dhammas, which Madhyamaka does not admit

equivalents.standpoint: P1-level: both name the level of worldly usage
equivalents.note: Advaita's vyāvahārika is the empirical level of a world superimposed on Brahman; Madhyamaka's saṃvṛti has no real substrate. Neither tradition accepts identity.

literal: the truth of the highest meaning, ultimate truth

definitions.definition: The truth in terms of the ultimate, which cannot be taught without relying on the conventional and without reaching which nirvāṇa is not attained (MMK 24.8–10); its mark is given in 18.9.
The nature found by correct seeing (MA 6.23); not within the domain of the intellect (BCA 9.2).
Twofold: the non-nominal ultimate beyond elaboration and the nominal ultimate accordant with it, object of reasoning.

cross_language.form: 勝義諦 shengyidi / 真諦 zhendi / 第一義諦 diyiyidi

equivalents.note: Theravāda paramattha denotes the ultimately real dhammas and nibbāna; Madhyamaka's ultimate is the emptiness of all dharmas
Advaita's pāramārthika is Brahman, a positive reality; Madhyamaka's ultimate is emptiness, which it refuses to reify. Both traditions reject identity.

definitions.definition: The ultimate, as in paramārtha-satya; Bhāviveka qualifies his negations as holding 'ultimately' (paramārthataḥ).
Conventional usage, in dependence on which alone the ultimate is taught (MMK 24.10); the Buddhas speak of arising and ceasing by worldly convention (ŚS 1).

literal: what is well known in the world, worldly consensus

definitions.definition: The conventional as accepted by the world without analysis; Candrakīrti admits conventional things on this basis only, not on the basis of own-characteristics.

Conventional things that arise from causes and function as they appear (e.g. water that quenches thirst), as against the incorrect conventional (mithyā-saṃvṛti) such as a mirage taken for water (Jñānagarbha); the ladder to the ultimate (Bhāviveka).
What satisfies only when not analysed, arises and ceases and is capable of function (MAL 64).
The ultimate accessible to reasoning — the negation of arising and the wisdom that knows it — accordant with the non-nominal ultimate (aparyāya-paramārtha) that is beyond all elaboration.
The negation of arising is called ultimate because it accords with the ultimate (MAL 70).

cross_language.note: opposite: rnam grangs ma yin pa'i don dam

literal: efficacy, capacity to perform a function

definitions.definition: Capacity to function as it appears, distinguishing the correct from the incorrect conventional (Jñānagarbha).
A mark of conventional things (MAL 64), adopted from Dharmakīrti's epistemology.
The four alternatives — is, is not, both, neither (or: from self, from other, from both, without cause) — each of which is rejected (MMK 1.1; 22.11; 25.17–18) or, in 18.8, used as a graded teaching.
Drawing out an unwanted consequence from the opponent's own position (e.g. that self-arising would be pointless and endless: Buddhapālita on MMK 1.1).
The proper method of the Mādhyamika, who, having no thesis, only shows the contradictions in others' positions; defended by Candrakīrti (PsP 1).
Insufficient by itself: a consequence-statement states no reason and example and, reversed, would imply an unwanted thesis (Bhāviveka).
One who establishes emptiness through consequences (prasaṅga) rather than autonomous inferences; a Tibetan doxographical name (thal 'gyur ba) for the line of Buddhapālita and Candrakīrti.

A formal inference with thesis, reason and example stated in one's own right, required of the Mādhyamika to prove emptiness (Bhāviveka: 'ultimately the inner sense-bases do not arise from themselves, because they exist, like consciousness').
Not appropriate for a Mādhyamika, who has no position of his own to establish (PsP 1).

cross_language.form: rang rgyud kyi rjes dpag / rang rgyud kyi sbyor ba

definitions.definition: Tibetan doxographical name (rang rgyud pa) for Mādhyamikas who use autonomous inferences — Bhāviveka and his followers, and the Yogācāra-Madhyamaka of Śāntarakṣita.
The Mādhyamika has no thesis of his own, so the faults of a thesis do not apply to him (VV 29).
One who has no position — existent, non-existent or both — cannot be refuted (CŚ 16.25); the great-souled have no position and no dispute (YṢ 50).

The Nyāya name for a debate in which one only refutes without establishing a thesis; the Mādhyamika's 'no thesis' stance (VV 29) was read by Naiyāyikas as vitaṇḍā, while the Mādhyamika holds that having no thesis is not a fault.
A negation that merely denies without implying any other positive thing; Bhāviveka takes the negations of arising in MMK 1.1 as of this kind.
Emptiness as the mere absence of own-nature is a negation of this kind (Tibetan exegesis of Candrakīrti).

cross_language.note: contrasted with ma yin dgag (paryudāsa-pratiṣedha), implicative negation

definitions.definition: The verbal-conceptual elaboration from which conceptual constructions, and from them action and afflictions, arise; it ceases in emptiness (MMK 18.5); reality is not elaborated by elaborations (18.9), and those who elaborate the Buddha do not see him (22.15).
An epithet of dependent origination (dedicatory verse) and of the ultimate (MMK 25.24): the stilling of all elaboration.

notes: The same compound ('prapañcopaśamaṃ śivam') describes the fourth in Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 7 (see brw:mandukya-madhyamaka-prapancopasama).

definitions.definition: Conceptual construction, from which action and afflictions arise and which itself arises from elaboration (MMK 18.5); reality is free of it (18.9).

Speculative views such as eternalism and annihilationism, rooted in accepting real existents (YṢ 46–48); emptiness is the relinquishing of all views, and the Buddha taught for their abandonment (MMK 13.8; 27.30).
The extreme that follows from 'it is': whatever exists by own-nature must be eternal (MMK 15.10–11; 21.14).

cross_language.form: rtag lta / rtag par smra ba

definitions.definition: The extreme that follows from 'it is not': to say that what existed before does not exist now entails annihilation (MMK 15.10–11); emptiness is not annihilation (17.20).

cross_language.form: chad lta / chad par smra ba

literal: one who says 'it is not'; nihilist

definitions.definition: The nihilist who denies action, its fruit and the other world; Candrakīrti argues the Mādhyamika is not a nāstika, since he teaches dependent origination and says only that things lack own-nature (PsP 17.30; 18.7).

Things do not arise from self, other, both or without cause (MMK 1.1); dependent origination is 'without arising' (dedication); non-arising taught in the Mahāyāna equals the extinction taught to others (RĀ 4.86).

equivalents.note: Gauḍapāda's doctrine of non-origination (Māṇḍūkya Kārikā 4) uses the same fourfold negation of arising; for Advaita it rests on the unborn Brahman, for Madhyamaka on emptiness — both would reject identity

definitions.definition: Reality, whose mark is to be not dependent on another, peaceful, unelaborated, non-conceptual and without multiplicity (MMK 18.9); those who do not know the two truths do not know it (24.9).
Reality is not within the domain of the intellect (BCA 9.2).
The nature of things, unarisen and unceasing, like nirvāṇa, where what is to be named and the domain of mind have ceased (MMK 18.7).
Suchness, a synonym of emptiness and reality in Madhyamaka usage (the way things are, without own-nature).

Not abandoned, not attained, neither annihilated nor eternal, neither ceased nor arisen (MMK 25.3); neither an existent nor a non-existent (25.4–10); not the slightest different from saṃsāra (25.19–20); the ending of the conceptions of existence and non-existence (RĀ 1.42).
Beginningless and endless (MMK 11.1), a three-pathed wheel of afflictions, action and birth turning like a firebrand's circle (RĀ 1.36); not different from nirvāṇa (MMK 25.19–20).

cross_language.form: 輪迴 lunhui / 生死 shengsi

definitions.definition: Liberation comes from the exhaustion of action and afflictions, which arise from conceptual construction and elaboration, which cease in emptiness (MMK 18.5); definite goodness (naiḥśreyasa) is liberation (RĀ 1.4).
The nirvāṇa of the Buddhas, who by great compassion do not abide in (a quiescent) nirvāṇa but remain for the good of all beings (Bhāvanākrama I).

cross_language.form: mi gnas pa'i mya ngan las 'das pa

definitions.definition: Desire, aversion and delusion arise from conceptualization in dependence on the errors about the pleasant and unpleasant; they do not exist by own-nature and so are not real (MMK 23.1–2); if they existed by own-nature they could not be abandoned (23.24).

The (four) errors of taking the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, the impure as pure and the selfless as self; the afflictions arise in dependence on them, and ignorance ceases with their cessation (MMK 23.1–2, 23.23; CŚ 1–4).

The first of the twelve links; the ignorant forms the formations, not the one who sees reality (MMK 26.10); ignorance is the conceiving of dependently arisen things as real (ŚS 64); saṃvṛti in the sense of what covers reality (PsP 24.8).

Action is intention and what is done having intended (MMK 17.2–3); it neither remains until ripening nor perishes into nothing, because it is without own-nature and unarisen (17.21); agent and action are established only in mutual dependence (8.12), like emanations (17.31–33).
Mental action; bodily and verbal action is what is done having intended (MMK 17.2–3).

A realist theory stated in MMK 17: an 'imperishable' like a debt-note connects action and fruit; it is abandoned only by cultivation (17.14–15). Nāgārjuna's own answer is that action, being unarisen, does not perish (17.21).

Grasping (the ninth link, fourfold: MMK 26.6) and the aggregates as what is appropriated by the appropriator; self and appropriation are explained like fire and fuel (10.15); grasping at nirvāṇa is a great grasping (16.9).

The five aggregates; the self is neither identical with them nor other than them (MMK 18.1), and the Tathāgata is not found among them in five ways (22.1); grasping at them is grasping at 'I' (RĀ 1.35).
If the person transmigrated it would be found when sought fivefold among the aggregates, bases and elements; it is not (MMK 16.2).

The self is neither the aggregates nor other than them (MMK 18.1); neither other than the appropriated nor identical with it (27.8); it is designated in dependence, like fire on fuel (10.15); the Buddhas taught self, no-self and neither (18.6).
Sought in seven ways like a chariot, the self is not found; it is a mere designation on the aggregates (MA 6.151ff).
Selflessness, taught by the Buddhas alongside the teaching of self and of neither (MMK 18.6); in the Mahāyāna twofold, of persons (pudgala-nairātmya) and of dharmas (dharma-nairātmya).
Its cultivation is better than the delusion of 'I'-making (BCA 9.78).

equivalents.note: Madhyamaka extends selflessness from persons to all dharmas, including the dhammas that Theravāda Abhidhamma treats as ultimately real

literal: view of the (real / transitory) collection as self

definitions.definition: The view that takes the aggregates as self and mine; all afflictions and faults arise from it, and the yogin refutes the self, its object (MA 6.120).

The sense and grasping of 'I'; with 'mine'-making it ceases when self and mine are pacified (MMK 18.2–4); grasping at aggregates brings 'I'-making, action and birth (RĀ 1.35); the aggregates arise from it (RĀ 1.29).
Grasping at things as 'mine'; when 'I' and 'mine' are exhausted, grasping ceases (MMK 18.4).

The Buddha, who is not found in the fivefold search as identical with or different from the aggregates (MMK 22.1, 22.8); he is without own-nature, as the world is without own-nature (22.16); nothing is said of his existence after death in any of the four ways (25.17–18).
The four conditions of the Abhidharma (causal, objective support, immediately preceding, dominant; MMK 1.2), which cannot contain the own-nature of the effect (1.3).
The four noble truths, which the objector says emptiness destroys (MMK 24.1) but which are possible only if things are empty (24.20); whoever sees dependent origination sees them (24.40).
All formations are deceptive in nature and therefore false; the Buddha said this to illuminate emptiness (MMK 13.1–2); formed by the ignorant, they are the root of saṃsāra (26.10).
Suffering is not produced by oneself, another, both or without cause (MMK 12.1); it is possible only as dependently arisen and empty (24.21).
Consciousness arises in dependence on the eye and visible form, as a son from his parents (MMK 3.7).
A simile, with dream and the city of the gandharvas, for arising, abiding and ceasing (MMK 7.34) and for sense-objects (23.8): things appear though lacking own-nature.
Simile for arising, abiding and ceasing (MMK 7.34) and for afflictions, actions, bodies, agents and fruits (17.33) and sense-objects (23.8).

An emanation produced by supernormal power; the agent is like an emanation and the action like an emanation's emanation (MMK 17.31–33); one magical man may stop another, as Nāgārjuna's empty words negate (VV 23).
Saṃsāra, whose three paths cause one another without beginning, middle or end, whirls like the circle traced by a whirled firebrand (RĀ 1.36).

notes: The same image gives its name to Gauḍapāda's Alātaśānti (Māṇḍūkya Kārikā 4); see brw:madhyamaka-to-gaudapada.

definitions.definition: Not elaborated by elaborations — one of the marks of reality (MMK 18.9).

The resolve to attain awakening for the sake of all beings; with compassion and non-dual understanding the cause of bodhisattvas (MA 1.1); twofold as aspiration and engagement (BCA 1.15–16); the elixir that turns the impure body into a Victor's image (BCA 1.10).
One of the three things in which the aspirant to omniscience must strive, after compassion (Bhāvanākrama I).
The awakening mind as wish, like one who wishes to go (BCA 1.15–16).
The awakening mind as engagement in the practices, like one who is going (BCA 1.15–16).
The awakening mind as the compassionate resolve for awakening for others' sake, cultivated by method; contrasted with the ultimate awakening mind (Bodhicittavivaraṇa; Kamalaśīla's tradition).

cross_language.form: kun rdzob byang chub kyi sems

definitions.definition: The awakening mind as the direct understanding of emptiness, free of the self of persons and phenomena (Bodhicittavivaraṇa; Kamalaśīla's tradition).

cross_language.form: don dam byang chub kyi sems

notes: Tengyur D3911 and D3912 are titled instructions on cultivating the conventional and the ultimate awakening mind (catalog:Derge-Tengyur:D3911, D3912); authorship not checked.

definitions.definition: One who, born of compassion, non-dual understanding and the awakening mind, travels the ten grounds to buddhahood (MA 1.1); one who is not a Buddha by own-nature could never become one (MMK 24.32).

The six perfections — giving, discipline, patience, vigour, meditation and wisdom — completed as ten with method, aspiration, power and knowledge and paired with the ten grounds (MA); wisdom is the purpose of the others (BCA 9.1).

equivalents.note: the Theravāda ten pāramīs list renunciation, truth, resolution, loving-kindness and equanimity where the Mahāyāna has meditation, method, aspiration, power and knowledge

definitions.definition: The first perfection; the bodhisattva gives away body, enjoyments and merit to all beings, then protects, purifies and increases them (ŚSK 4); respectful giving is part of the dharma of higher status (RĀ 1.10).
The second perfection; the ten white paths of action (RĀ 1.8–9); guarded by guarding the mind (BCA 5.1).
The third perfection: there is no austerity equal to patience and no evil equal to hatred (BCA 6.2).
The fourth perfection: delight in the good, opposed by laziness, attachment to the base, despondency and self-contempt (BCA 7.2).
The fifth perfection: settling the mind in concentration through solitude, seeking calm first, then insight (BCA 8.1–4).
The sixth perfection, understanding emptiness; all the other practices were taught for its sake (BCA 9.1); chief of faith and wisdom, though faith comes first (RĀ 1.5).
Method — compassion and the perfections of giving and the rest — which must be united with wisdom (Bhāvanākrama II); conventional truth is the means to the ultimate (MA 6.80).

Compassion, praised first as seed, water and ripening of the Victors' harvest; threefold as focused on beings, on dharmas (impermanence) and without object (MA 1.2–4); the root of buddhahood (Bhāvanākrama I); out of compassion the Buddha taught for the abandonment of all views (MMK 27.30).
The root of all the qualities of buddhahood and the cause of the Buddhas' non-abiding nirvāṇa (Bhāvanākrama I).
The friendly mind which, with self-restraint and benefiting others, is dharma, the seed of fruit here and hereafter (MMK 17.1); part of the dharma in brief (RĀ 1.10).
The practice, cultivated first, of regarding all beings as equal to oneself in wanting happiness and not wanting suffering, protecting them as oneself (BCA 8.90–96; ŚSK 1).
The 'supreme secret' by which one quickly protects oneself and others: taking others as oneself and giving oneself to others (BCA 8.120, 8.136).
The teacher who guides the bodhisattva; not abandoning the spiritual friend is part of protecting the body for beings' benefit (ŚSK 6).
The two collections: merit (puṇya), from which the form bodies arise, and wisdom (jñāna), from which the truth body arises (RĀ 3.12–13).
Turning one's merit to the welfare and awakening of all beings — the tenth chapter of the Bodhicaryāvatāra (10.55–56).
Confessing before the Buddhas the evil done in beginningless saṃsāra and this life, with remorse and resolve (BCA 2.28ff).
Happiness in good rebirths, the fruit of the dharma of higher status practised first (RĀ 1.3–4).
Liberation, reached gradually after higher status; its dharma is subtle and frightening to the childish (RĀ 1.3–4, 1.25–26).
The Tathāgatas describe the Dharma in brief as non-harming, and nirvāṇa as emptiness (CŚ 12.23); non-harming is part of the dharma of higher status (RĀ 1.10).
Faith goes first and wisdom is chief (RĀ 1.5); the root to be made firm before setting the mind on awakening (ŚSK 2).
The rope with which the elephant of the mind is bound (BCA 5.3).
Repeatedly examining the state of body and mind (BCA 5.108).
Heedful guarding of the awakening mind once adopted — the subject of Bodhicaryāvatāra ch.4.
Calm, to be sought first, through solitude and delight free of worldly attachment; insight together with calm destroys the afflictions (BCA 8.4).
One-pointed calm, developed by removing laxity and excitement, on which insight is based (Bhāvanākrama).
Insight arising from the correct analysis of reality (bhūtapratyavekṣā), joined with calm (Bhāvanākrama).
Insight united with calm destroys the afflictions (BCA 8.4).

literal: analysis of what is real / correct discernment

definitions.definition: Analysis by wisdom of the nature of things; without it non-recollection and non-attention cannot lead to non-conceptuality (Bhāvanākrama III).

cross_language.form: yang dag par so sor rtog pa

definitions.definition: The wisdom entered when, analysing, the yogin finds no dharma arisen in the three times; it pacifies all elaboration and penetrates emptiness (Bhāvanākrama III).
When neither being nor non-being remains before the mind, it is pacified without object (BCA 9.35).

cross_language.form: rnam par mi rtog pa'i ye shes

definitions.definition: Scriptural 'non-recollection and non-attention' mean the result of analysis finding nothing to recollect; mere absence of mental activity is like fainting and is not non-conceptual wisdom (Bhāvanākrama III).
The reason by which Śāntarakṣita proves that things lack own-nature: they have neither a truly single nor a truly manifold nature (MAL 1).
Consciousness is self-aware by nature, its not being inert; accepted conventionally (MAL 16–17).
Rejected even conventionally: mind does not see mind, as a blade does not cut itself (BCA 9.17ff; MA 6.72ff).
Accepted as the account of conventional reality — external objects do not exist — before understanding that mind too lacks self (MAL 92–93).
The sūtra's 'mind only' denies a creator other than mind, not external form; teachings denying external objects are of provisional meaning (MA 6).
The truth body of the Buddhas, born from the collection of wisdom (RĀ 3.12–13).
The form bodies of the Buddhas, arising from the collection of merit (RĀ 3.12–13).
One whose knowledge arises without a teacher when no Buddha appears and the śrāvakas have passed away (MMK 18.12); a 'middle buddha', born from the Buddha's teaching (MA 1.1).

cross_language.form: 辟支佛 pizhifo / 緣覺 yuanjue

definitions.definition: The intellect is conventional; reality is not within its domain (BCA 9.2).

The creator posited by others is refuted: if he creates without wishing he depends on another, if by wishing he depends on his wish (BCA 9.119–126); an eternal cause would produce all effects at once or never (Tattvasaṅgraha).

literal: the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in its cause

definitions.definition: Refuted as arising 'from itself': an effect already existing would arise pointlessly and endlessly (MMK 1.1 with Buddhapālita; Madhyamakahṛdaya 6).

The means of knowledge are established neither by themselves (as fire does not illumine itself) nor by other means (infinite regress) nor by their objects (VV 31–51); Nāgārjuna apprehends nothing by them and so affirms or denies nothing (VV 30).
Perception and inference as defined by Dharmakīrti, used to establish momentariness, emptiness and omniscience at the conventional level (Tattvasaṅgraha).
Objects of knowledge and means of knowledge are established only in mutual dependence, and so neither is established by own-nature (VV 46–51).
The objector holds that perception establishes things (VV 5); Nāgārjuna answers that he apprehends nothing by perception to affirm or deny (VV 30).
Autonomous inference is required to establish emptiness (Bhāviveka).
Only inference acceptable to the opponent (paraprasiddha) and consequences are used (Candrakīrti).

Non-dual understanding (advaya-buddhi), free of the extremes of existence and non-existence, is with compassion and bodhicitta a cause of bodhisattvas (MA 1.1); the non-dual path to nirvāṇa (PsP 17.30).
The ten bodhisattva grounds from the Joyous (pramuditā) to the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā), each marked by the predominance of a perfection (MA chs. 1–10).
